1: Practical eleven and twelve: multivariate analysis in Python. We implement K means for structure discovery, compute the silhouette score, and visualise groups with pairplots, on the Superstore Retail Orders dataset.
2: Setup. Besides pandas, numpy, seaborn and matplotlib, there are four new imports this lab: variance inflation factor from statsmodels, standard scaler for feature scaling, K means for clustering, and silhouette score for cluster quality. Then we load the C S V and drop the rows where segment is missing.
3: Select the numeric features, same pattern as practical nine and ten. We pick all numeric columns and drop postal code, which is an I D. The result is sales, quantity, discount and profit, and all four are used together throughout this lab.
4: Step one of the multicollinearity check: the correlation matrix and heatmap. Df of numeric cols dot corr, and a seaborn heatmap with annotations. This is a quick first check. Look for any cell close to plus one or minus one between two different features. Here no pairwise correlation is strong, which is a good first sign.
5: Step two: computing V I F. We set X to the numeric columns, build a table with the feature names, and then for each column compute variance inflation factor of X values and index i. There is no single vectorised command for this, so we use a short list comprehension, the standard idiom for V I F in Python. The results: sales one point three six, quantity one point zero four, discount one point zero six, and profit one point three seven. All four V I Fs sit close to one, well under the moderate threshold of five, so it is safe to use all four features together in the clustering.
6: K means step one: scale the features. X scaled equals standard scaler dot fit transform of the numeric columns. Standard scaler rescales every feature to mean zero and standard deviation one. Fit transform learns the scaling from the data and applies it in one step, returning a plain numpy array. Without scaling, sales, up to twenty two thousand six hundred thirty eight dollars, would completely dominate discount, which ranges from zero to point eight, and K means would end up clustering on sales alone.
7: K means step two: implement K means for structure discovery. We create K means with n clusters equal to three, random state forty two, and n init ten. Looking for three groups, we check why three on the next slide. Random state forty two makes the result reproducible run to run. N init of ten runs from ten random starts and keeps the best result. Fit predict fits the model and returns each order's group in one step, which we store in a new column called cluster. Value counts shows three very different group sizes, about sixty nine hundred, two thousand, and one thousand seventy orders, hinting that these are genuinely different kinds of orders and not an arbitrary split.
8: Choosing k with the silhouette score. This is the one place in the lab where a loop is the simplest way, comparing several candidate values of k in turn. For k from two to six, we fit K means and print the silhouette score. The scores are point five oh four, point four seven three, point four three one, point four three seven and point three eight. K equals two scores highest, but k equals three, a close second, gives three clearly interpretable groups, so we proceed with three.
9: Visualising the groups. A scatterplot of sales against profit with hue equals cluster colours each point by its assigned group. The pairplot with vars equal to the numeric columns and hue equals cluster shows every feature pair, all coloured by cluster, in one command.
10: Naming the groups with grouped statistics. Df dot groupby cluster, then numeric columns, dot mean, rounded to two decimals. Cluster zero: six thousand nine hundred nine orders, everyday orders. Cluster one: one thousand sixty eight orders, average discount point six six and average profit of minus one hundred six dollars, heavy discount and loss making. Cluster two: two thousand seventeen orders, average sales six hundred thirty four dollars, high value and high profit. Then we cross tabulate the clusters against category, with row percentages, as a sanity check.
11: A worked example on a second dataset, Titanic, with the same pattern. We compute V I F for age, fare, sibsp and parch, scale them, fit K means with three clusters, compute the silhouette score, and summarise with group by. All four features come back with V I F close to one, so no multicollinearity. The silhouette score for k equals three is about point four eight, similar to the Superstore result. One cluster is older, high fare passengers with few family members aboard. Another is younger passengers travelling with larger families. The third is mid age, low fare solo travellers.
12: Lab code cheat sheet. For multicollinearity: the correlation matrix with a heatmap, and the V I F list comprehension. For K means: scale with standard scaler, fit K means with your chosen k, a random state and n init, store the cluster labels, and compute the silhouette score. To visualise and interpret: a scatterplot with hue equals cluster, a pairplot with hue equals cluster, and group by cluster with mean.
